questions.stem: Explain what site means for a settlement's location.

answer.exemplar: Site is the physical character of a place itself, such as its terrain, climate, and resources, independent of its surroundings.

questions.explanation: Site refers to the internal physical attributes of a location. Situation, by contrast, concerns relative position.

questions.explanation: Situation is about relative position and connections. It differs from site, which is the place's own physical character.
questions.hint: Relative location and connections.

questions.topic: Land consumed by a dispersed pattern
questions.learningObjective: Compare dispersed and compact land use
questions.stem: The clerk's note compares 100 houses on 50 hectares versus 100 houses on 10 hectares; which is more compact?
questions.explanation: The 10-hectare development houses the same 100 houses on less land, so it is more compact. Compactness means less land per unit.
questions.hint: Less land for the same houses means compact.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: The clerk's note asks for a benefit of compact growth; which applies?
questions.explanation: Compact growth lowers infrastructure costs per person by concentrating development. It consumes less land and raises density.
questions.hint: Concentration lowers infrastructure costs per person.

questions.topic: Why agglomeration pays and what it charges
questions.stem: The clerk's note asks for a cost of agglomeration; which applies?

options.misconception: names a benefit, not a cost
names a benefit, not a cost

questions.explanation: Agglomeration costs include congestion and higher rents. Knowledge spillovers and shared suppliers are benefits.
questions.hint: Congestion and rents are costs of clustering.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Why a watershed is a management unit
questions.learningObjective: Apply watershed management to a case

stimulus.body: The clerk's note considers managing water by political boundaries rather than watershed boundaries; the memo warns this may fail.

questions.stem: Why might political boundaries fail as water management units?

options.text: Watersheds are too small to matter
They are always better than watersheds
They may split a watershed, ignoring upstream-downstream links

questions.explanation: Political boundaries can split a watershed, breaking upstream-downstream management links. Watersheds follow natural drainage instead.
questions.hint: Political lines can cut across natural drainage.
